Meet the Peaky Blinders, Ukraine's drone unit protecting devastated front-line city

The dangers in Slovyansk are clear from the start.

"If I say run, you run," Tetiana tells us. She and her colleague Yasha are escorting us into a city now under constant bombardment from Russian drones, missiles and glide bombs.

It is raining and cloudy as we enter the city, and our military escorts call this "good" weather, meaning it is bad for drones.

But the threat is still there, and Yasha keeps his eyes peeled on the skies, while 21-year-old Tetiana scours her phone for the latest military intelligence on likely threats from the air.

They are members of a drone unit who call themselves Peaky Blinders and their distinctive emblem is a flat cap of the type made popular by the cult BBC TV series, although theirs are camouflaged.

Slovyansk is one of four cities that make up Ukraine's "fortress belt" - a system of heavily reinforced defence lines in the parts of eastern region of Donetsk still under its control.

Russia wants Kyiv to give up the fortress cities and they are central to talks on a possible peace deal that have resumed after nine months between Ukraine, Russia and the US in Abu Dhabi.

Ukrainians worry that doing so would make it much easier for Russia to advance further west, including to the capital Kyiv.

Very little of the city has been left unscathed by months of heavy bombardment

Once inside the city, we leave our vehicles hidden under the cover of trees and venture out on foot. Yasha carries a shotgun – a last resort to shoot down Russian drones. In halting English, Tetiana tells us walking is safer than travelling by car.

Abandoned vehicles litter the streets – recently destroyed by remotely operated Russian first-person view drones. The anti-drone netting that covers the roads is no guarantee of safety.

Tetiana shows us a video on her phone taken a few days earlier.

You can hear several drones buzzing above her, and then the cacophony of small arms fire as Ukrainian forces try to shoot them down. Tetiana admits it can be scary but explains how she felt compelled to help her country, abandoning her dreams of becoming an opera singer.

Slovyansk is now a husk of its former self. Very few buildings have been left unscathed, with many reduced to rubble.

Tetiana shows us a school recently destroyed by Russian glide bombs. Across the road there is a gaping hole in an abandoned residential block. Broken glass litters the pavement. The few shops still functioning are boarded up – making it hard to distinguish what is still open. Most have closed.

Tetiana says the Russians are doing everything they can to intimidate people and drive them out of the city. That, she says, "is their strategy – to make people leave in chaos, gathering up their last belongings and fleeing amid enormous fear and suffering. They want people to have nowhere left to live".

It is a familiar pattern already seen in other Ukrainian towns and cities in the Donbas – like Pokrovsk and Bakhmut. These are now ghost towns reduced to rubble, but eventually falling into Russian hands.

Russia has already taken nearly 90% of the Donbas – made up of the regions of Luhansk and Donetsk - but its advances this year have all but stalled in the face of strong Ukrainian resistance.

The White House is sounding positive about the revived talks in Abu Dhabi, despite Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky's refusal to cede the territory.

October was the deadliest month for Russian troops since the start of its full-scale invasion – with more than 54,000 killed or injured, according to Ukraine's general staff. Despite this, Russian forces are still making life in the Fortress Belt cities almost impossible.

Iryna, who works in one of the city's last remaining cafes, is one of the few residents who decided to stay

Before the war, Slovyansk was a city of more than 200,000 people. Less than 10% of those remain and the population diminishes by the day.

But amid the wail of near constant air raid warnings, there are still signs of people clinging on to life here. Iryna works in one of the city's last remaining coffee shops. Slovyansk is where she was born.

"I'm forced to walk around crying," she tells me. "How can they do this?"

Life, she says, has become incredibly difficult. She has already lost her house. But despite her tears, there is still defiance: "I won't leave Slovyansk. This is my home."

Inga, 53, was also born and raised here and continues to work in the city despite the danger.

"It's stressful. Honestly, I don't even know what to say," she says, but she is staying because of what she calls the "fear of the unknown".

"I simply have nowhere to go, and I don't have the money to leave or support myself afterwards." Nor, she says, is there anywhere else in Ukraine she would consider truly safe.

Commander Oleksandr of the Peaky Blinders special forces unit says neither side is able to advance because of the large number of drones in use

We first met the Omega National Guard Special Forces drone unit two years ago fighting in the Kharkiv region, in north-eastern Ukraine.

Just four of the original team remain - the rest have moved to other units, or they have been wounded or killed.

Among the dead was the brother of the man in charge of the unit, Oleksandr, who now describes his unit as his family.

He jokes it is just like the Peaky Blinders TV show – "but without the crime and the drugs". Back at their base they share a meal every evening.

Oleksandr reads out a prayer of thanks for surviving another day – he says it strengthens their spirits. The meal is accompanied by classical music played on a speaker. It helps drown out the noise of the explosions nearby.

"I feel this is the most difficult situation we've ever faced," says Oleksandr, who underlines the importance of holding the line.

"We must be here to inflict maximum damage on the enemy. We're fighting here because this is where the most intense phase of the war is taking place. Russia's claim that they will reach the borders of the Donbas, seize it, and then the war will end is absolutely false," he insists.

The remaining fortress belt cities provide Ukraine with a strong defensive line and are a major obstacle to any Russian advance. The saturation of drones in the area is also now making it nigh-on impossible for either side to advance here.

Peace talks may have resumed, but Oleksandr notes they have not led to anything so far.

"I really want this war to end," he says, "but do I believe these negotiations will succeed? No, I don't really believe they will".

The streets are largely empty, with increasing numbers of residents evacuated as drone attacks intensify

The next morning we are not the only ones making an exit. A dozen civilians have arrived at an evacuation point in the centre to be escorted out.

They hold all the belongings they can carry and are taken into a bunker for their safety. Outside there is another heavy blast of small arms fire, signalling more drones are nearby.

Alina Shyrko, herself a resident of Slovyansk, is co-ordinating the move of civilians out of the city and says the situation has deteriorated rapidly over the past few months. Families with children have already been ordered to leave.

"Everyone is thinking about leaving," she says, "I'm thinking about it too."

Ukraine still holds Slovyansk but its lifeblood, its people, are ebbing away.

McTominay reveals he underwent heart procedure days before World Cup game

Scott McTominay says he received treatment to correct an irregular heartbeat two days before Scotland's World Cup win over Haiti in June.

The Napoli midfielder recently underwent an ablation procedure - a minimally invasive operation to correct irregular heart rhythms - in Manchester.

At the World Cup, the 29-year-old was was put to sleep to correct his heartbeat and given the all-clear to play in the opening 1-0 victory over Haiti in Massachusetts.

"I had to go and get the shock on my heart," revealed the former Manchester United player, who also played 90 minutes in the losses to Morocco and Brazil.

"It was two days before the Haiti game. You've prepared so well. I was in such good condition and then something like that happens. You're thinking, 'how is this happening to me?'

"You have to get on with it, that's the cards that you're dealt in football. Sometimes, things don't go your way.

"I was 100% [fit], but obviously, whenever you're sat in a hospital bed two days before the first game of the World Cup about to get put to sleep, it's not ideal, is it?"

McTominay praised his club and the medical staff who treated him in the autumn.

He missed Scotland's opening four Nations League fixtures - a win, a draw and two defeats - but has been recalled to the squad after returning to domestic and Champions League action with Napoli.

Sebastien Pocognoli's side host North Macedonia on Friday and visit Switzerland on Monday.

"Yeah, I'm good," said McTominay. "I'm feeling much, much better than what I was. I feel like it was something that needed to be done. In your career, you have moments like that where things can take you a bit by surprise.

"Obviously, it looks a lot worse to people in the media and family and friends who reach out to you after they see news related to a heart issue, but it's a relatively straightforward procedure, which went really, really well in Manchester.

"So just really happy to be back and playing football again. That's the most important thing in my life and it always will be in terms of wanting to come back and prove myself again and making sure that I can go to another level."

Nations League: Scotland v North Macedonia

McTominay added: "For me, it's always about coming back stronger.

"No matter how well you play in one game, it's about the next game and pushing yourself and recovering well and eating the right things, sleeping correctly throughout your career."

Barcelona are the reigning Women's Champions League title holders

The total prize pot available for clubs participating in the 2026-27 Women's Champions League proper is €18.2m (£15.2m), with €7.7m (£6.4m) on offer for participation in the qualifying rounds.

Uefa will also pay out €5.6m (£4.7m) to teams in the Women's Europa Cup, and a further €6.2m (£5.2m) in 'solidarity payments' to national associations that have at least one club participating in the Champions League.

The €18.2m Champions League prize pot has been in place since 2025, and will increase to €24.1m from 2027 to 2030.

Before any games are played, a guaranteed participation fee of €505,000 (£422,500) is paid to all 18 clubs that qualified for the league phase, with 75% paid as a down payment.

Performance-based money is then allocated as follows:

Final league phase ranking bonus: €10,000 (£8,200) per place (eg €10,000 for 18th, €180,000 for first)

Knockout phase play-offs: €100,000 (£83,700)

The knockout play-off, quarter and semi-final payments are given to both clubs participating.

The 'solidarity payments' are then made to clubs in top domestic women's leagues that did not take part in the Champions League proper.

These payments vary depending on the performance of the national association's club or clubs that took part in the Champions League.

Uefa state that the national associations must distribute their solidarity payments equally among clubs in their top domestic women's championship that did not qualify for the tournament, including those knocked out in qualifying and those taking part in the Europa Cup.

The rules also state these payments must be "earmarked for development purposes and may not be used for the fixed and ordinary costs of the club".

Uefa has also announced that the first €2m (£1.7m) of any surplus amounts (once sales are finalised) will be split between clubs participating in the league phase, with the remainder divided between league phase, qualifying and Euorpa clubs as well as solidarity payments.

Eddie Howe, Mauricio Pochettino and Unai Emery have all been linked with replacing Michael Carrick as Manchester United boss

With one victory in their first 10 Premier League matches, Manchester United have made their worst start to a top-flight campaign since the 1986-87 season.

They are 18th in the table, one point above bottom club Crystal Palace .

United directors will meet in Monaco on Wednesday to discuss Michael Carrick's future as his 10-month spell as head coach comes under major scrutiny.

If the 45-year-old former player departs, it would mean an eighth permanent boss for the Red Devils since Sir Alex Ferguson retired 13 years ago.

That would be as many managerial changes as they have made across the previous 68 years dating back to Sir Matt Busby's appointment in 1945.

BBC Sport takes a look at the leading candidates who could replace Carrick.

Mauricio Pochettino penned a new deal with with the USA in the summer

Major trophies won: 1 Ligue 1, 1 French Cup

Premier League record: P294, W150; Win percentage: 51; Points per game ratio (PPG): 1.77

Did you know: Pochettino averaged 1.89 points per game during his spell at Tottenham , the best ratio of any Spurs manager to have taken charge of 25 or more Premier League games.

United's long-standing interest in the Argentine, 54, dates back a decade.

At Spurs , he moulded their best team in a generation, but ultimately came up short of winning a trophy, losing both the Champions League and League Cup finals, and posted second and third-placed finishes. Silverware did come at Paris St-Germain with a league title, but a spell at Chelsea proved tougher with a League Cup final defeat by Liverpool in 2024.

Having led the USA to the last 16 of the World Cup on home soil he signed a new contract taking him up to the 2030 tournament. Pochettino has an exciting group of young players to work with for the national team - led by Manchester City -bound 17-year-old Cavan Sullivan - but he has always made it clear he has unfinished business in the Premier League.

A reported buyout clause in Pochettino's contract is worth $10million (£7.44m), while it is also understood to contain clauses that would allow him to leave for specific high-profile jobs.

Julian Nagelsmann resigned in the summer after Germany lost to Paraguay on penalties in the World Cup

Did you know: Only Hansi Flick (88.9%) has a better win percentage by a Bayern Munich manager in the Champions League than Nagelsmann's 83.3%.

Nagelsmann first impressed with his work at Hoffenheim, where he became the youngest head coach in Bundesliga history aged 28, leading them from relegation struggles to the Champions League.

He followed that by taking RB Leipzig to a Champions League semi-final in 2020 and Bayern Munich understandably came calling.

But despite winning the Bundesliga title in his first season he reportedly fell out with key players and did not survive a full second season.

In 2023, Nagelsmann took charge of a Germany side in transition, and they were narrowly beaten in the quarter-finals of Euro 2024 by eventual winners Spain, but stepped down in the summer after Die Mannschaft were humbled by Paraguay in the World Cup last 32.

Still only 39, his reputation may have taken a bit of a hit, but the German is still regarded as one of Europe's best coaches. Manchester United 's director of recruitment Christopher Vivell also knows him well, having worked together at RB Leipzig.

Eddie Howe oversaw more Premier League wins (84) than any other Newcastle manager

Premier League record: P369 W140; Win percentage: 37.9; PPG: 1.36

Did you know: Eddie Howe (five) is one of only three managers with five or more wins against Mikel Arteta in all competitions, along with Pep Guardiola (11) and Jurgen Klopp (six).

His body of work in English football needs little introduction having led Bournemouth to the top flight for the first time in their history, before he confirmed his place in Newcastle folklore with their first major domestic trophy since lifting the FA Cup in 1955.

The League Cup final triumph over Liverpool was one of the greatest days in the club's history, while he also secured two top-five finishes to take the club back into the Champions League for the first time in 20 years.

Howe, 48, left in the summer after an underwhelming 12th-placed finish last term and Newcastle would only be due a a relatively small amount of compensation should he be tempted by the Old Trafford job.

Antonio Conte called Tottenham's players "selfish" when he left after 16 months in 2023

Major trophies won: 5 Serie A, 1 Premier League, 1 FA Cup

Premier League record: P132, W83; Win percentage: 62.9; PPG: 2.03

Did you know: Chelsea won 30 of their 38 Premier League matches as they claimed the title in Antonio Conte's first season in charge in 2016-17.

A serial winner, Conte's managerial credentials are not in doubt.

He left Napoli of his own accord this summer just 12 months after delivering only the fourth top-flight title in their history.

That added to Serie A triumphs at Juventus (three) and Inter Milan, and spells at Chelsea and Tottenham .

Conte, 57, would appear to be a no-brainer of a choice to take over at United, but could the Italian's fiery nature and history of falling out with clubs count against him?

His last stint in English football ended under a cloud of controversy as he left Tottenham in 2023 following criticism of the players and the club's culture.

While he had success at Chelsea , Conte also reportedly clashed with both players and the board.

Emery has also managed Arsenal and Paris St-Germain in his career

Major trophies won: 5 Europa League, 1 Ligue 1, 2 French Cups, 2 French League Cups

Premier League record: P200, W101; Win percentage: 50.5; PPG: 1.75

Did you know: Unai Emery has the best Premier League win percentage (51%) and points per game ratio (1.75) of any permanent Aston Villa boss.

Vastly experienced, the Spaniard's stock is at an all-time high courtesy of the superb job he has done since taking over at Villa in October 2022.

Having taken the club into the European Cup/Champions League for the first time for 41 years, the 55-year-old then ended their 30-year wait for silverware with success in last season's Europa League.

Despite having lost the spine of his team over the summer, Emery's new-look side are finding their feet again and the chances of him leaving for United look even slimmer with recent news he is expected to sign a new contract.

Michael Carrick's Manchester United side have managed one win in 10 league games this season

Premier League record: P29, W14; Win percentage: 48.3; PPG: 1.76

Did you know: After his initial appointment as United's interim boss in January, Michael Carrick had the most wins (12) and points (39) of any Premier League manager during the rest of the 2025-26 season.

Still clinging on to his job in the Old Trafford hot seat, could United's hierarchy actually decide to keep faith with Carrick?

After such a brilliant start and end to the season following his arrival in January, the wheels have come off spectacularly this term with only three wins from 15 matches in all competitions.

His team have at least shown fight with comebacks in recent games to beat Roma and salvage a point in a 4-4 draw with Aston Villa , but their overall stats are damning and the outlook doesn't look good for the 45-year-old, who won five Premier League titles and the Champions League as a United player.

The club are in the relegation zone and 18th is their lowest position after 10 games of a season for 40 years. It is also only the second time they have gone eight Premier League games without a victory.

Burnt out and crushed vehicles were strewn across the motorway in the aftermath of the crash

Twelve people have been killed after dozens of cars and lorries were involved in two pile-ups on the Trakia motorway in south-eastern Bulgaria, Prime Minister Rumen Radev has said.

Health Minister Katya Ivkova said 11 people died at the scene on Tuesday, near the town of Zimnitsa, while another person later died in hospital. About 50 others were taken to hospital with injuries.

Sliven regional governor Mihail Kasherov told journalists that more than 70 vehicles were involved in the incident, Bulgarian state news agency BTA reported.

Officials have said dense fog reduced visibility and was the likely cause of the first crash, which occurred on the eastbound carriageway.

Radev declared Wednesday a day of national mourning following the incident.

The second crash, on the Sofia-bound carriageway, was likely also caused by the fog, with drivers also distracted by the first crash, BTA reported an official as saying.

The Trakia motorway runs from west-to-east of Bulgaria, and connects the capital Sofia to the Black Sea coast.

Road administration director Galin Kostov added that speeds were unsuitable for the conditions, which included wet road surfaces, and the motorway would remain closed until it had been cleared, BTA reported.

Yambol regional governor Georgi Chalakov said reports first came in at 07:10 local time (05:10 GMT), with the injured taken by ambulance to hospitals in the Yambol, Sliven and Burgas regions.

Chalakov told BTA rescue teams had to remove sections of the crash barrier to reach people. He added that the fog meant that helicopters could not be used in the evacuation efforts.

A drone captured the scene from above, just visible through the dense fog

One witness who helped rescue a man from a burning vehicle blamed "very thick fog" for the pile-up.

"I got out of the car, I ran forward and pulled that man out," the witness told Reuters news agency.

Another told Reuters that "many, many people died".

"As for me, there were four cars behind me - trucks - and I don't know how I got out or what happened, but in the end, thank God I'm still alive," that witness said.

Radev - who had been hosting European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen - cut short a news conference after learning of the incident and visited the scene.

Heavy rain and stormy weather made life harder in Gaza, says resident

US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace has called on Israel to immediately allow all necessary humanitarian supplies into Gaza after rain flooded tens of thousands of tents.

The US-backed body, established to oversee the implementation of Trump's Gaza peace plan, acknowledged the steps now being considered by Israel, but said "the response remains insufficient".

Israel's military agency in charge of co-ordinating aid into Gaza said it had allowed in tens of thousands of tents and trucks with winter supplies, but added reconstruction "can only begin after Hamas fully disarms".

On Sunday, three children and a woman were killed when a sand embankment collapsed onto tents in the central Strip.

Most people in Gaza have been displaced because of Israel's military actions. Around 65% of the population, about 1.4 million people, now live in tents or makeshift shelters, the UN says.

Standing soaked in Gaza City, Mohammed Jneid told the AFP news agency that heavy rains hit from one side and sewage overflowed on them from the other, with the ground and tents no longer able to hold.

"We have nothing left, no bedding, no food, nothing," he said.

Sitting inside her tent, Islam Al Mobayed told AFP there were seven children there, five of them young.

"This is not life," she said. "We are exhausted, we are tired of this entire life."

In rare criticism of Israel, the Board of Peace said it had been urging the Israeli government to authorise the entry of essential goods for temporary shelter and water and sanitation infrastructure.

The Board added that delays in approving the entry of supplies "exacerbated the consequences of a foreseeable humanitarian challenge" and delayed the start of decommissioning weapons and transferring Hamas authority to a transitional government.

It also said Hamas's failure to disarm and transfer power had compounded the difficulties facing Gaza's civilians.

The UN's humanitarian agency OCHA said more than 150,000 tents were outside Gaza ready to go in, but aid efforts were constrained "by Israeli restrictions on the entry of supplies and equipment and funding shortfalls".

UN humanitarian coordinator Ramiz Alakbarov said on Monday that stocks of essential shelter and winter items inside Gaza had been exhausted.

"Israeli authorities must immediately lift all restrictions on entry of the supplies," he said, adding "we have run out of time".

Israel's foreign ministry spokeswoman Michal Maayan on Monday said Israel had in recent months put in place a winter plan in coordination with the Board of Peace and international charities.

That plan has brought in more than 91,000 tents and 8,200-plus trucks with tarpaulins, blankets, winter clothing, and other equipment, according to Cogat, the Israeli military body responsible for aid.

Cogat said it would not allow in equipment that could be used for military purposes.

Maayon accused Hamas of hoarding aid, saying: "Hamas is responsible for the delays in making more progress in the Strip, and winter-related hardships are a consequence of Hamas's action and policy."

In response to the Board of Peace, Hamas said in a statement published on Palestinian media that its comment "presents a distorted account of the causes of the disaster". The group denied it was responsible for ceasefire delays, pointing to a statement in August , external from Egyptian, Qatari and Turkish mediators that accused Israel of violations.

Hamas said Israeli restrictions prevent the entry of materials necessary for shelter and recovery - and added the Board as the ceasefire implementor should look at its own "serious shortcoming".

Under the deal to end the two-year-long war in October 2025, Hamas agreed to give up governance and its weapons in exchange for a phased Israeli troop withdrawal from the 60% of Gaza it still occupied. Israel, however, has insisted Hamas must fully disarm before withdrawal.

The dispute has left the next stages of the peace plan stalled, with both sides blaming each other.

The war in Gaza began after the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023 when around 1,200 people were killed and 251 others taken hostage.

The Israeli military campaign in response has killed 74,645 people, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures the UN considers reliable. More than 1,600 people have been killed since the ceasefire in October last year.

Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza since then.

David Walliams has been accused of grooming young fans and harassing women in the workplace, after failing to stop the Guardian and ITN publishing claims against him.

A three-year investigation , external by the two news organisations alleged the Little Britain star and former Britain's Got Talent judge preyed on teenage girls as young as 15 and young women , external for sexual purposes.

He had sought a High Court injunction to prevent publication, with his lawyers arguing if allegations were made public Walliams would likely kill himself. The court refused the request.

Walliams has denied all of the allegations but in a letter to journalists working on the investigation acknowledged "at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with".

He added: "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me."

The 55-year-old became a household name in the early 2000s through Little Britain, his comedy sketch show with Matt Lucas broadcast on the BBC.

Walliams published his first children's book, The Boy in the Dress, in 2008, and his stories soon became best-sellers and led to comparisons with Roald Dahl.

His 23 children's books have sold more than 50 million copies worldwide, but he was dropped by publisher HarperCollins in 2025 after allegations of inappropriate behaviour, which he denied.

In 2012, Walliams became a judge on Britain's Got Talent, and was voted best TV judge at the National TV Awards (NTAs) four times. He was replaced as a judge in 2022.

Before entering showbusiness, Walliams was born David Williams but changed his surname's spelling to avoid having the same name as another member of entertainment union Equity.

He was married to Dutch model Lara Stone from 2010 to 2015 and they have a son.

That hasn't stopped speculation about Walliams' sexuality. He has described himself as "bi-curious" and called his 2012 autobiography Camp David – but said he isn't attracted to men in the way he is to women.

Matt Lucas and David Walliams as Florence and Emily in Little Britain

Walliams and Lucas won a string of awards for Little Britain including three Baftas and two International Emmys, and the programme was watched by 10 million people in the UK.

But in the two decades since it ended, views about the show and what is and is not acceptable to joke about have radically altered. The programme has been criticised for its use of blackface and for stereotyping and mocking characters from minority and marginalised groups.

In the wake of the Black Lives Matter movement in 2020, Little Britain was removed from streaming services including BBC iPlayer, Netflix and BritBox.

Another of the duo's shows, 2010 airport comedy Come Fly With Me, was also removed from BritBox a decade after its original broadcast, due to the show's use of racial stereotypes and using make-up to portray people from other ethnic groups.

Little Britain was restored to iPlayer in 2022 with several scenes cut out. Walliams and Lucas said they had re-edited the show to "better reflect the changes in the cultural landscape since the show was made".

Walliams won the National Television Award for best TV judge four times for Britain's Got Talent

Not all the criticisms of Walliams have involved new standards being applied to older work.

Walliams had to apologise after two charity performances, during which he yanked down not only the trousers but also the underwear of actor Jeremy Edwards and music producer Mark Ronson.

In 2020, he was booed while hosting the NTAs after making a joke about Caroline Flack being out of work, at a time when she had stepped down from hosting Love Island and was waiting to appear in court, having been charged for actual bodily harm following a row with her boyfriend.

Later in 2022, he was replaced as a judge on Britain's Got Talent after a Guardian story about a leaked recording of Walliams making insulting remarks about contestants during breaks from filming.

In the incident, which happened in 2020, he spoke about a pensioner to whom he had taken a strong dislike and a woman who he described as "the slightly boring girl you would meet in the pub" who "you would want to have sex with, but then decide not to". He used much stronger language when talking about both.

Walliams apologised, explaining: "These were private conversations and - like most conversations with friends - were never intended to be shared. Nevertheless, I am sorry."

He sued the show's producers Freemantle for misuse of his private information and breaching data protection laws. An "amicable resolution" was reached, with the production company apologising for the recording being made public.

Walliams raised more than £3m for the Sport Relief charity by swimming the English Channel in 2006 and the length of the River Thames in 2011.

Further controversy came in June 2025, when it emerged that Walliams had given two Nazi salutes during the recording of BBC One's Would I Lie to You? Christmas special.

Banijay UK, which owned the show's production company Zeppotron, apologised, adding: "It was immediately acknowledged during the recording that this segment would not be broadcast under any circumstances." Walliams has never commented on the incident.

Then in December 2025, HarperCollins, the publisher of his hugely successful children's books, announced that following a change of CEO, the company would no longer look after new releases by Walliams.

He was dropped over allegations he had harassed female members of staff, with HarperCollins explaining that the company took "employee wellbeing extremely seriously and has processes in place for reporting and investigating concerns".

The Daily Telegraph reported that an internal investigation had been opened the previous year after a complaint was made by a junior member of staff about his behaviour. This reportedly found that staff had been told to only meet Walliams in pairs and advised against going to his house.

Walliams' spokesperson responded by saying he "strongly denies that he has behaved inappropriately" and that he had "never been informed of any allegations raised against him" by the publisher.

Then in September 2026, HarperCollins doubled down by announcing that they were cutting all ties with Walliams and would no longer represent his back catalogue, meaning that when his books sold out in shops, they would not be replaced.

Watch: Cleaning, shirt swaps & video games - the Charles bros at home

Pierce Charles can't help but smile as he waits for Shea to walk into the kitchen.

It's Shea's 23rd birthday and he has a cake to surprise him, something he knows will embarrass his older brother.

Right on cue, he gets the response that he was looking for as Shea has a sheepish smile, and Pierce launches into a rendition of 'Happy Birthday' for the cameras.

In an exclusive interview at their London home, the brothers talk about breaking lamps while playing football as kids, debating who does the chores and the upcoming release of video game Grand Theft Auto VI.

With a cup of tea offered and shoes off at the door, you wouldn't think you were chatting with two international footballers, especially two who are riding the crest of a wave on the pitch.

London traffic aside, they are enjoying life in the hustle and bustle of the city as they live in England's capital for the first time.

"It's better than I thought it was going to be, I didn't think I was going to enjoy it," said Pierce who is spending the season on loan at Queens Park Rangers from Manchester City.

"I actually love it, and living together has been good. There's so much to do in London," added midfielder Shea, who joined Fulham from Southampton in a £30m move in August.

Using international football to reignite Premier League dreams

NI win in Georgia after Kvaratskhelia penalty miss

It is the first time the brothers have lived in London, but the third time they have lived together.

Having been born and grown up in Manchester, they came through Manchester City's academy before Pierce joined Sheffield Wednesday aged 16.

Shea stayed at the Etihad and made his Premier League debut under Pep Guardiola in May 2023 before signing for Southampton that summer.

The brothers were reunited at Wednesday when Shea joined on loan for the 2024-25 campaign, but there was some 200 miles between them last year as the midfielder returned to St Mary's.

This summer, after impressive performances for Wednesday and Northern Ireland, Pierce returned to Manchester City in a long-term deal before joining QPR on loan.

Not to be outdone, Shea earned a switch back to the Premier League with Fulham as he became Northern Ireland's first £30m footballer.

Both based in west London, that gave them the opportunity to move back in together, reigniting debates over who is better at the Grand Theft Auto games and Fortnite and who cooks the better steak sandwich.

They both want to claim top honours, but Pierce feels he will have the edge if he can get the peppercorn sauce recipe off the chef at QPR.

Older brother Eoin and parents Mary and Kelvin often come to visit, too, and there's more debate over who makes the house presentable, and whether doing the dishwasher actually counts as a chore.

"I think she secretly wants it to be messy, so she can have a little dig at us and do it anyway," jokes Pierce about Mary, who was born in Northern Ireland.

"She enjoys it really, she's not on holiday," Shea laughs.

Quickly realising the danger of getting a telling off on her next visit, Shea adds, "Mum is class. We appreciate mum".

Things quickly get competitive between the brothers over a game of two touch

Before the brothers sit down for a chat, there's time for a kick about in the garden for a game of 'two touch'.

It doesn't take long for their competitive side to shine through, and a best of three quickly becomes best of five then, eventually, a rematch.

Conversation turns to memories of similar games in the family garden as kids and how things used to always take a similarly competitive turn.

"When we used to play Wembley I would have always beaten you two and the loser went in nets," said Shea.

"If you want a fun fact, people might think he is the best player now but Shea was actually the worst out of us when we were younger in the back garden," Pierce was quick to respond.

"It was me, then Eoin and then Shea. To be fair, he's improved massively since."

There's a blame game over a broken clock and lamp, and middle child Shea has to plead his innocence over the latter.

"I broke the clock but I didn't break the lamp. It actually wasn't me, I swear," recalled Shea, still pleading his case before a mischievous "I loved that lamp" almost makes him look guilty.

Fourteen years on from watching the Olympics, Pierce Charles made a late double save to earn QPR a draw at West Ham's London Stadium

The brothers have yet to hit London's tourist spots since moving to the capital, but a trip to Thorpe Park just outside the city is on the cards.

Their first memories of London are from visiting their cousins growing up, and there have been trips to Wembley to see childhood club Manchester City.

But the London 2012 Olympics stand out as an early memory, when the brothers would have been eight and nine years of age.

They remember meeting Team GB heptathlete Katarina Johnson-Thompson and recall racing outside of the London Stadium.

"There were little events on outside the stadium," Shea recalled.

"Like the 50 metres and that sort of stuff. I won my race."

Now the home of West Ham United, both brothers have played at the ground this season, some 14 years on from watching the Olympics at the same venue.

When QPR visited West Ham in October, Pierce was the hero as he saved Jarrod Bowen's last-gasp penalty to deny the Hammers three points.

His man of the match trophy from that game is proudly displayed in their home.

"It looks so much different from what I remember," said Shea on the London Stadium.

"And then we're playing in it 14 years later," added Pierce.

"It's mad, we're getting on a bit aren't we?"

Pierce and Shea Charles both had big moments as Northern Ireland won in Georgia in September

The Charles brothers are just two players in a young and exciting Northern Ireland squad.

Michael O'Neill's side currently top Group B2 in the Nations League after four matches, and they have yet to concede a goal.

The campaign started in Georgia in September and both Shea and Pierce played their part in a famous win.

Pierce saved a penalty from Paris Saint-Germain star Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, and also made another big intervention to deny Georges Mikautadze.

Then, nine minutes into additional time, Shea popped up with a late winner to kick-start a window that would see Northern Ireland top their Nations League group after four matches, without conceding a goal.

"I think that's what started the good run," said Pierce.

"You can't win a game like that and fall off."

Highlights: Northern Ireland leave it late to beat Georgia

Now, Northern Ireland will look to finish the job as they host Ukraine in Belfast on Saturday, and finish the campaign in Hungary on 17 November.

"Two wins would be the dream and it would set us up nicely for the next few years," said Pierce.

"The next few games will be tough but we can't wait."

Given they live together and will be in Northern Ireland camp side-by-side - do they get sick of each other?

"It feels like I can't get away from you when we're on camp, but at least it's not shared rooms," said Shea.

"We're just joined at the hip," said Pierce, who added he doesn't get fed up with spending time with his brother.

"We're always together but we're not always together, if you know what I mean."

Hundreds of women have come forward with abuse allegations against the former Harrods and Ritz Paris owner

French police have made arrests after three properties, including the Ritz hotel in Paris, were searched in relation to an investigation into Mohamed Al Fayed's abuse.

The Paris prosecutor's office told the BBC that several individuals were taken into custody for questioning last month and later released.

In a confidential letter sent to survivors, the Metropolitan Police said its officers were present during the searches on 13 and 14 October, in what is understood to be a joint operation between British and French authorities.

It is the first time any arrests have been made in relation to alleged abuse and trafficking by the former Harrods and Ritz owner.

Mohamed Al Fayed accused of multiple rapes by staff

Several victims of Al Fayed were also interviewed by French investigators, the prosecutor's office said.

It added that the searches were part of a preliminary investigation into "allegations of human trafficking committed by an organized group, aggravated pimping committed by an organized group, and rape".

The investigation is ongoing and digital material seized during the searches is being analysed.

The late Egyptian billionaire bought the Ritz Paris hotel in 1979, and it is still owned by the Al Fayed family.

The Villa Windsor in western Paris, another property involved in the search, was a holiday home for the Al Fayed family. It was previously the home of King Edward VIII, following his abdication, and his wife Wallis Simpson.

The Met shared this statement from French authorities with victims:

"At this stage of the proceedings, several victims have been interviewed by French investigators, and the investigations are being conducted in liaison with the British authorities.

"In this context, searches and evidence-gathering operations were carried out in mid-October 2026, notably within the Hotel Ritz in the 1st arrondissement of Paris, as well as at the Villa Sainte-Thérèse in Saint-Tropez, a former property of Mohamed Al Fayed, and at the Villa Windsor in the 16th arrondissement of Paris, in the presence of British investigators.

"Several suspects were taken into police custody, measures which were lifted following their interviews, specifically for the purpose of analyzing digital material seized during the search operations.

"The investigations are continuing under the direction of the Paris Public Prosecutor's Office."

A Met Police spokesperson confirmed its officers travelled to France in October and were present during the operation.

The Ritz hotel in Paris is still owned by the Al Fayed family

Al Fayed, who died in 2023 aged 94, was accused by more than 20 women of sexual assault in a BBC documentary and podcast in September 2024.

One of the women featured in the documentary said she was sexually assaulted by Al Fayed at the Ritz hotel in Paris, while another woman said she had been raped by him at the Villa Windsor residence.

Since those allegations, more than 400 alleged victims or witnesses have come forward to lawyers.

A woman has also told BBC Scotland she was trafficked, drugged, sexually assaulted and held prisoner on the Balnagown Estate by Al Fayed's brother , Salah Fayed, who died in 2010.

Both brothers died without facing legal charges in relation to these allegations.

Earlier this year, Police Scotland said it was carrying out further investigations into allegations connected to Balnagown Estate.

In a statement, a force spokesperson said: "Three people have been identified in connection with offending against a number of victims.

"Our inquiries are ongoing and it would be inappropriate to comment further."

The Justice for Fayed and Harrods Survivors group said it welcomed the "significant developments" and cooperation between the Met and French authorities.

"We believe that all properties owned by Fayed should be investigated with the same thoroughness as those already searched, wherever they are located, to ensure that no potentially relevant evidence is overlooked," the group said.

"We hope these developments represent meaningful progress towards identifying and holding to account all those who facilitated, concealed or assisted his offending, wherever they operated."

The survivor advocacy group No One Above said: "France is treating this as organised human trafficking, led by specialists, with properties searched and evidence seized. That is what a serious investigation into a network looks like.

"Two years on, survivors are still waiting for the same from the Met. It is time the National Crime Agency took this investigation over."

The management of the Ritz Paris told AFP news agency that it "does not tolerate any form of harassment, abuse or inappropriate behaviour" and that it was ready "to cooperate fully with the competent judicial authorities".

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support is available at BBC Action Line .

Head coach Vincent Kompany has returned to Bayern Munich's training ground after collapsing at the end of last month.

The 40-year-old former Manchester City captain was taken to hospital after falling ill while watching the club's second team train.

Kompany was diagnosed with meningeal irritation - an inflammation of the protective membrane surrounding the brain and spinal cord.

Bayern said in a statement: "Vincent Kompany is on the road to recovery and has been back at the training ground since the start of the week."

However, the Bundesliga leaders did not hold a training session, with most players away on international duty.

English coach Aaron Danks has been in charge during Kompany's absence, leading Bayern to four victories and a draw.

They face Cologne next on 20 November after the end of the two-week international break.

Kim Bjorkegren (right) is in interim charge of Ghana after Carlos Queiroz left the Black Stars by mutual consent

As Ghana prepare for two make-or-break 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) qualifiers with women's coach Kim Bjorkegren in temporary charge, former boss Chris Hughton has called for greater consistency in the Black Stars dugout.

The West Africans face Somalia in back-to-back fixtures over the next week, having lost their first two games in Group C against Ivory Coast and The Gambia last month.

Those defeats resulted in the departure of Carlos Queiroz, whose brief period in the hot seat was characterised by uncertainty.

The Portuguese's exit means Swede Bjorkegren, who has been in charge of the Black Queens since January 2025, has now been asked to lead the men's team against Somalia.

"When you have inconsistency in the amount of time when a manager is staying, it's never good," Hughton told BBC Sport Africa.

"You want that consistency in the players [and] the players want that consistency in what they see in the manager."

Queiroz, who had two spells as Sir Alex Ferguson's assistant at Manchester United, was initially appointed in April and led Ghana to the last 32 of the Fifa World Cup, holding England to a goalless draw in the group stage, before announcing his own departure shortly after the team were eliminated 1-0 by Colombia in the last 32.

However, the 73-year-old was reappointed in early September, with the Ghana Football Association (GFA) praising his "extensive international experience" gained during time in charge of South Africa, Egypt, Portugal, Iran, Colombia, Qatar and Oman.

But Queiroz's return lasted less than a month following a 2-0 defeat by the Ivorians in Bouake and a 4-2 humbling against the Gambians in front of home fans in Accra.

"What I saw in the World Cup is that they represented the country very well, particularly the England game," said Hughton.

"And although it was very much a defensive outfit, there were opportunities to score."

Hughton, however, admits that regular sackings can create an "attitude" within a squad, with players knowing that "if he (the coach) doesn't do well then he won't be there".

Ex-Brighton boss Hughton reveals cancer diagnosis

Ex-Brighton boss Hughton backs mental health drive

Ghana suffered group-stage exits at the 2021 and 2023 Afcons under Milovan Rajevac (left) and Chris Hughton (right) before failing to qualify for the 2025 edition under Otto Addo (right)

Hughton's Ghana reign was also short lived.

Appointed as technical director by the GFA in February 2022, he moved into the head coach role in February 2023 but lasted less than 12 months before being sacked in January 2024 after his team failed to get out of their group at the 2023 Afcon in Ivory Coast.

The former Ireland full-back, who won two FA Cups and a Uefa Cup with Tottenham Hotspur and coached Newcastle, Norwich and Brighton in the Premier League, is one of five men who have taken on the Ghana job in the past six years.

Charles Akonnor, Milovan Rajevac, Otto Addo and Queiroz are the others, with the chopping and changing further illustrated by the fact that Addo had two spells in charge during that time.

Kwesi Appiah, the current Sudan boss, lasted 33 months during his second stint with the Black Stars between April 2017 and January 2020 - the longest anyone has managed since legendary Afcon-winning coach Fred Osam-Duodu in the late 1970s and early 80s.

With Ghana in real danger of missing out on a second successive Afcon finals, Hughton believes the situation has been exacerbated by under-investment and what he describes as "fearsome" competition across the continent.

"Many years ago Ghana were at a level that was, if not the best team in Africa, certainly right up there," said the 67-year-old.

"You've seen the emergence of so many other good African nations that have made the competition levels that much higher.

"Some of these countries have so many other problems, but I do think that there needs to be an injection of government money into the structure and into the system."

Hughton feels more needs to be done to encourage the development of the game in the West African nation.

"In Ghana, the local game that used to produce so many good players, the support level is not there," he said.

"They're playing on pitches that are not of a great level and the supporters are not coming.

"The supporters in Ghana love the Black Stars most, first and foremost, and of course the Premier League is massive there, but there isn't that support for the local game that there used to be.

"I think the government needs to do more as regards putting money into the infrastructure."

Coventry City midfielder Caleb Yirenkyi scored the only goal as Ghana beat Panama at the World Cup in June

While Ghana have failed to make it past the second round of Afcon since 2017, the country's World Cup record is far more impressive.

They have qualified for five of the past six finals since their debut in Germany in 2006, reaching the knockout stage on three occasions including a quarter-final appearance at the 2010 tournament in South Africa.

Having cruised through qualification for this year's World Cup in Canada, Mexico and the United States, losing only one of 10 games as they topped their group under Addo, Queiroz could reasonably claim he was hamstrung by multiple withdrawals ahead of his first Afcon qualifiers.

Six players named in the original squad, including Antoine Semenyo, Mohammed Kudus, Jordan Ayew and Baba Rahman, dropped out, followed subsequently by some of those called up as replacements.

Hughton hopes it is a situation which is not repeated - and which was not caused by the uncertainty around Queiroz's position.

"Whether that was a reason or not, I don't know. And I probably don't think so," he stated.

"You always want your best players and it's always a concern to the level of the group when you have so many players pull out.

"There isn't too much you can do about that [and] you have to work around that."

With the team's chances of reaching next year's Afcon in East Africa in serious peril, a lot rests of the shoulders of interim coach Bjorkegren.

As Ghana's long wait for a first continental title since 1982 continues, finding some long-term stability in the Black Stars' coaching set-up would be a good first step.

US inflation rose at a faster-than-expected pace in October, according to official figures.

Prices rose by 0.4% in the month, which was lower than the 0.6% increase in September.

However, analysts had expected prices to rise by 0.3%, and the higher-than-expected pace could add to arguments for the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates at its next meeting in December.

The new figures come a week after the midterm elections which were fought over cost-of-living pressures across the US.

Inflation is the rate at which the price of products or services increases over time.

For example, if a bottle of milk costs $1 but rises to $1.10 a year later, then annual inflation for bottled milk is 10%.

Officials from the Bureau of Labor Statistics measure inflation through the consumer price index (CPI).

It tracks the price changes of hundreds of day-to-day items including fresh food, gasoline and medical services to work out the overall level of inflation in the US economy.

The bureau updates this so-called basket of goods over time as peoples' spending and lifestyle habits change.

There are several factors that can cause inflation to rise.

If demand for a product outstrips its supply, that can lead to producers raising prices - the craze for Labubu dolls in recent years and the high resale prices are an example.

Higher incomes can also lead to higher demand, for example, which in turn pushes up prices.

Supply and demand: Labubu dolls illustrate how inflation can rise

Supply can also affect inflation. If supply of a product is reduced, but demand remains constant, that can cause prices to rise. A good example of this is crude oil, which is used to make gasoline and diesel.

Before the US-Israel war with Iran began, it was trading at just over $70 a barrel, but when the conflict constricted crude supplies, the price quickly rose and is currently over $100.

Over the month of October, prices rose by 0.4%, driven by increases in housing, food and energy costs.

However, the pace of energy price rises, at 0.7% in October, was much lower than the 5.2% increase seen in September.

While the Bureau of Labor Statistics would normally provide figures for the 12-month change in prices, it did not collect data in October 2025 so it could not provide that estimate.

For the 12 months to September, inflation was 3.7%.

The US Federal Reserve has a target for keeping annual inflation at 2%.

When inflation is too high the Fed tends to raise interest rates in order to encourage people and businesses to save more and spend less money in the hope this will slow price rises.

While there was no annual figure published for inflation this month, analysts say the fact inflation was higher in October than expected increases the chance of an interest rate rise at the Fed's December meeting.

Federal Reserve governor Chirstopher Waller, who spoke before the latest inflation figures were published, also suggested he was leaning towards a rate increase in December even if October's figures were slower than expected.

US interest rates held steady and economy grows - what it means for you

Since coming into office for the second time, President Donald Trump has introduced tariffs on most US trading partners around the world.

While most of the additional global levies were outlawed by the Supreme Court in February, the president immediately announced a new 10% global tariff to replace them.

Trump argued the tariffs would increase America's tax earnings, boost manufacturing and encourage people to buy US-made goods, but the higher import taxes have also had an impact on inflation, according to research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.

US President Donald Trump raised tariffs

Higher tariffs - which are levies that businesses pay on the goods they import - directly raise prices for US companies unless the overseas firms they are buying from lower prices to absorb some of the cost.

In response to the new tariffs, the New York Fed found exporters reduced prices very little, meaning US-based businesses ended up absorbing nearly 90% of the cost of the added tax.

Indirectly, higher tariffs also affected the prices of locally made goods, as many US producers rely on parts or materials from overseas.

Overall, the Fed found that every percentage point increase in average tariffs led to nearly a 0.25% price increase for consumer goods after one year.

While inflation is currently above where the Federal Reserve would like it has been much higher in previous years.

During the Covid pandemic, issues such as supply chain disruption started pushing inflation up.

Additionally, in early 2022 when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, oil prices surged over $100 a barrel.

Both of these factors helped to drive inflation to a peak of about 9%.

It's important to note that if inflation is rising at a slower rate, that does not mean prices are going down - it simply means prices are rising at a slower pace.

A bit of inflation is considered good for an economy as the Federal Reserve's target rate illustrates.

Many central banks consider inflation of about 2% or a little higher to be stable, and at a level that doesn't impact people's purchasing decisions.

Much below that, people can delay spending if they expect price rises to slow further, or to fall. That can lead to businesses reducing wages, or reducing the number of workers to cope with lower demand.

The value of social security benefits is changed to largely keep up with inflation, protecting people's ability to purchase their usual goods and services through the cost-of-living adjustment.

Shortly after September's inflation figure was released, the Social Security Administration announced that Social Security benefits including old age, survivors and disability insurance would rise by a similar amount - 3.6% - in 2027.

The administration said that the 3.6% rise will mean an average retirement benefit increase of $75 a month.

The cost-of-living adjustment will take effect in January for about 72 million people, while increased payments for the 7.2m receiving the supplemental security income will start on 31 December.

KIGALI – Homepoint, the trade name of Hotpoint Appliances Rwanda Ltd., has opened its fourth showroom at Kimironko, a store dedicated exclusively to the Haier brand.

The opening on Monday, 9 November 2026, marks another milestone in Homepoint’s long-standing commitment to shaping Rwanda’s home appliance market by leading with quality, service and innovation.

Supported by Homepoint’s product advisors and after-sales service team, the Kimironko outlet joins Homepoint’s established stores in Kicukiro, Remera and KIC, bringing customers in one of Kigali’s busiest residential and commercial areas simultaneously.

Closer to Haier’s portfolio of refrigeration, laundry, cooling and kitchen appliances, visitors can compare models, receive expert advice and arrange delivery in one place.

Founded in 2010, Hotpoint Appliances Rwanda has spent more than fifteen years building its reputation as one of the country’s most trusted appliance distributors and solutions providers.

Through Homepoint, the company represents internationally respected brands including Haier, LG, Philips, Kenwood, Black&Decker, Kent RO, Hawkins, Brabantia, VON and Daikin.

Homepoint has consistently chosen to compete on product quality, reliability and long-term customer value rather than on price alone.

That philosophy is delivered through a complete customer ecosystem spanning retail showrooms, the homepoint.rw online store, business-to-business supply, engineering solutions and after-sales support.

The aim is to ensure that every customer who buys from Homepoint should enjoy the product for years, backed by professional installation, maintenance and service.

Murli Menon, the Chief Executive Officer of Hotpoint Appliances Rwanda, says this focus on quality and service is what Rwandan consumers obviously expect.

“Today’s consumers are increasingly prioritizing quality, reliability, and value. Our role is to bring internationally trusted brands to Rwanda while ensuring customers receive world-class service and support. Our consumers are discerning, informed, and seek products that deliver lasting value,” he said.

Partnering with the World’s Leading Appliance Brand

After securing official distribution rights, Hotpoint Appliances Rwanda committed to giving Rwandan households direct access to the brand’s innovative products through a dedicated Haier Brand Store.

According to Euromonitor International, Haier was the world’s leading major appliances brand by sales volume in 2025, the 17th consecutive year it has held that position.

Menon noted that Haier’s strong combination of quality and affordability has so far resonated well with Rwandan customers, and the dedicated showroom allows shoppers to experience the brand’s technology first-hand before they buy.

Consolee Nshimiyimana, Head of Retail at Homepoint, says the change is visible on the showroom floor.

“As more Rwandans invest in building modern homes, demand is shifting from conventional freestanding cookers toward integrated kitchen solutions. Customers are increasingly choosing built-in appliances such as microwaves, ovens, and cooker hoods to achieve both functionality and modern aesthetics,” she said.

She added that today’s customers arrive better informed and focused on performance, energy efficiency and long-term value, which is why Homepoint invests in product training so that its advisors can guide every purchase.

Recognizing that affordability remains a key consideration for many households, Homepoint is working with a newly launched Microfinance company FlexiPay, a customer-friendly financing solution that will allow eligible customers to spread payments over two, three, four or six months.

Manoj Skariah, Managing Director of Hotpoint Appliances Rwanda, said the aim is to make quality appliances accessible without compromising on standards.

“FlexiPay is designed to simplify the purchasing journey. Customers can visit our showroom, choose the product they want, select a payment plan that suits their needs, and receive a financing decision within a short timeframe,” he explained.

The program is expected to launch before end of November.

Homepoint’s commitment to quality is equally visible in its engineering division, which has delivered air-conditioning and ventilation projects for major institutions.

Its solutions feature energy-efficient inverter technology and environmentally friendly R32 refrigerants, supported by professional installation, maintenance and after-sales service.

With Kimironko now open, Homepoint plans to introduce other showrooms in Musanze, Rubavu and Gahanga as part of its long-term growth strategy, bringing its standard of quality and service to more Rwandan households.

As consumer expectations continue to rise, Homepoint’s formula of trusted global brands, expert advice, accessible financing and dependable after-sales support puts it at the forefront of Rwanda’s expanding quality home appliance market.

The Kimironko Haier Brand Store is the newest showcase of that promise.

MN202611_th1lpktj46.t:
Steven Pressley, John McGlynn and Steve Clarke have all been mentioned in despatches

Another season, another managerial sacking at Aberdeen.

Stephen Robinson's departure on Monday made it five dismissals since the spring of 2021.

The Northern Irishman followed Stephen Glass, Jim Goodwin, Barry Robson and Jimmy Thelin in making an abrupt exit on the watch of chairman Dave Cormack.

Most of the quintet have lasted less than a year and, although Thelin ended the Dons' 35-year wait to win the Scottish Cup, the general trend has been one of perceived underachievement in Scottish Premiership.

Derek McInnes, now with Rangers after spells at Kilmarnock and Heart of Midlothian, was the last Pittodrie boss to regularly deliver consistent results in the top flight and consequent European qualification.

So who could be next? And what qualities does such a manager require?

'Aberdeen hunt yet another manager after ill-fated Robinson reign'

Aberdeen sack Robinson after league slump

Falkirk add goals and grit to McGlynn's guile on rapid rise

Two names mentioned fairly early on after Robinson's exit were Dundee's Steven Pressley and Falkirk's John McGlynn .

Both have impressed in the Premiership this past 17 months, drawing admirers for style of play and good results.

Falkirk are third in the division, two places above Dundee, and McGlynn's side were sixth last season, again two places higher than Pressley's men.

Former Aberdeen defender Richard Foster said the pair are "the two that stand out for me domestically" and said of Elgin-born Pressley on BBC Radio Scotland's Breakfast: "I know he's got a quiet, laid-back demeanour, but I think in the dressing room, he commands respect.

"The players at Dundee seem to love playing for him.

"He knows the game very well. Having played at Hearts, having played at Celtic, he knows what it's like to be at a huge club."

Former Hearts, Hibernian and Scotland midfielder Michael Stewart has been impressed with McGlynn's track record of signing players.

Speaking on McGlynn on BBC Radio Scotland's Sportsound, Stewart said: "John McGlynn puts the miles in.

"He's up and down the road down south. He's up and around all over Scotland. He knows what the players are that are perhaps not in the eye of many others. He knows them intimately before they arrive at Falkirk.

"So it's no great surprise that his success rate with recruitment is pretty, pretty good.

"I would not be surprised if, whenever one or two of the bigger jobs start coming up... rather than being sort of an outsider, I think he'll be right in the hunt for some of those jobs."

Former Celtic and Hibs midfielder Scott Allan says McGlynn is "very tactically astute" and commented: "I love everything that John McGlynn does. Everybody in Scottish football can respect the job he's done there, the consistency.

"He's one of the most prepared managers, if not the most prepared manager for any sort of set-up that he faces week-to-week and he's shown that.

"It's a fantastic job he's done over the last three or four years. He deserves all the credit that comes his way."

It may seem like a lifetime ago, but it's actually only been five months since Steve Clarke stepped down as Scotland head coach.

The 63-year-old, like McGlynn, has vast coaching experience, including in Scotland after a two-year spell with Kilmarnock.

Clarke oversaw three qualifications to major tournaments with Scotland, ending long waits to appear at the European Championship and World Cup.

As well as managerial stints at West Bromwich Albion and Reading, Clarke has worked at Chelsea, Liverpool and Newcastle United, so little would daunt the former right-back.

Appointing Clarke would be a statement by Aberdeen and the challenge of restoring the club to competitiveness may be a compelling one for the man himself.

However, along with McGlynn, geography may play a part and their candidacy could depend on whether personal circumstances allow a switch to the north east.

Wigan Athletic boss and former Scotland centre-half Gary Caldwell has also been linked with the Pittodrie job. The 44-year-old cut his managerial teeth with the Latics and returned there earlier this year after spells in charge of Chesterfield, Partick Thistle and Exeter City.

Swede Thelin stands out as one of the few overseas managers Aberdeen have had.

Yes, Goodwin and Robinson hail from Ireland and Northern Ireland respectively, but both are very much embedded in Scottish football after spending so much time at various clubs north of the border.

The only other non-Scottish manager to grace the Pittodrie home dugout was the Dane, Ebbe Skovdahl, from 1999-2002.

As such, it is fair to say Aberdeen have not experimented too much with foreign coaches and have tended to go with faces familiar to the Scottish top flight.

With a German, Lutz Pfannenstiel, as the sporting director, Aberdeen look further afield this time?

It has become the vogue in the Premiership of late, with Hearts, Hibs and Motherwell going foreign, with Belgian Wouter Vrancken, Dutchman Marink Reedijk and Swede Alfred Johansson in recent months.

Should Pfannenstiel unearth the next Jens Berthel Askou, formerly of Motherwell, Dons fans will be delighted.

Former Aberdeen defender Stuart Duff is in interim charge of Aberdeen following the departures of Robinson, assistant Brian Kerr and coach Stephen Craigan.

The Dons are second bottom of the Premiership, two points above Kilmarnock.

Unless an appointment is made during the international break, Duff faces taking Aberdeen to face Kilmarnock on 21 November before visiting Rangers three days later, with their next home game being against Dundee on 28 November.

Confidence is low after seven league defeats so far this season, but the tightly-packed middle section of the league means Aberdeen are only a couple of wins off the top six.

Solange Alexandre twice turned down the Légion d'Honneur before relenting in 2024

One of France's last Resistance heroes from World War Two has died at the age of 104. Solange Alexandre was also a rare woman who, with her future husband, created and commanded her own unit of anti-German fighters.

After serving as a Resistance courier from 1941, three years later she founded the Pas-de-Boeuf network near the town of Ruillé-sur-Loir.

With some 30 men under her orders, she organised sabotage operations, sheltered Allied airmen and, after the Allied landings in Normandy on D-Day in 1944, joined the fight against the occupying German forces.

President Emmanuel Macron was among many to pay tribute to Alexandre, after her death was announced at a nursing home in Le Mans.

"She said she only ever did her duty. But her duty was our freedom. France will never forget. Thank you," Macron posted on social media.

Born in 1922 in the Sarthe department of western France, Solange Alexandre, née Dubuisson, grew up in a patriotic family that had suffered in World War One.

"My mother lost her first husband in the war, and my father was wounded in 1917. The words homeland and honour were very important to us. They were in my blood," she recalled in her memoirs.

In June 1940 she heard on the radio the appeal from General Charles de Gaulle in London, calling on the French not to give up the struggle against Germany. She had never heard of him, but that did not matter.

"From that moment I knew I had to join up," she wrote.

Some months later she was recruited by a friend of her father's – a Tunisian-born French army veteran called Saïd Belhaffaf, who had joined the Resistance.

Using the code-name Corlay, she criss-crossed the region around Le Mans by bicycle, gathering information and passing on messages.

"There were no mobile phones back then, and no private cars either because of the lack of petrol. The bicycle was king," she said in an interview two years ago.

In 1943 she met her first husband Guy Déliot, who had deserted from the French gendarmerie after refusing to arrest some Jews.

The following April, with the Allied invasion approaching, they decided to take to the maquis, in other words live clandestinely in the forested hills, supplied with food by local farmers.

Their group consisted of deserters from German forced labour programmes, as well as survivors from another Resistance outfit that had been destroyed by the enemy. There were also two airmen, one American and one Canadian.

"Twice the Gestapo came for me, and twice I slipped through their hands," she later recalled.

After taking part in the liberation of Tours in September 1944, she ended the war with the rank of sub-lieutenant in the French Interior Forces (FFI).

Later she worked as a teacher and followed her husband on his many postings as an officer of the gendarmerie in French overseas territories. He was killed in 1960 in Martinique, and in 1981 she remarried.

Twice Solange Alexandre turned down the Légion d'Honneur , saying that she had only done her duty and that others were more worthy.

On receiving the award she said: "It is a great pleasure and a great honour. I am very proud – even if it is only a few weeks, or a few months, before I die."
